Currently, 5,609 patients are receiving treatment at different hospitals across the country.

item.title: Banks to raise awareness against cyber fraud in export transactions
item.description:
Bangladesh Bank has instructed all Authorized Dealers (ADs) of foreign exchange, mainly banks, to raise awareness among exporters regarding preventive measures against cyber fraud in export transactions, particularly those involving the electronic exchange of information and documents.
The Foreign Exchange Policy Department-1 (FEPD-1) of the central bank issued a circular letter (FEPD-1 Circular Letter No. 22) in this regard on Monday, addressed to the head offices and principal offices of all Authorized Dealers in Bangladesh.
Signed by FEPD-1 director Nasima Sultana, the circular noted that recent media coverage has drawn attention to the growing risks of cyber fraud in business communications, including the manipulation of export documents and fraudulent alterations to payment instructions.
To safeguard against such threats, the central bank advised ADs to sensitize exporters on four key precautionary measures:
Special care must be taken when transmitting export documents directly to foreign buyers under general authorization, ensuring secure communication channels are used to minimize the risk of interception or manipulation.
Any changes in buyers’ or sellers’ bank account details or payment instructions must be independently verified through previously established contact channels before being acted upon.
Exporters must avoid suspicious links, unverified applications, and requests for passwords, PINs, or One-Time Passwords (OTPs).
Any suspected fraud, unauthorized change in payment instructions, or manipulation of export documents must be reported promptly to designated ADs.
Bangladesh Bank also requested the banks to disseminate these precautions among exporters through appropriate communication channels.

item.title: NBR extends online VAT return deadline by a week
item.description:
The National Board of Revenue (NBR) has extended the deadline for online submission of October 2026 value-added tax (VAT) returns by seven days after server complications disrupted its electronic filing system.
Under the extension, VAT-registered taxpayers can submit their October returns through the NBR’s electronic VAT (eVAT) system until November 22 without incurring any interest or penalties.
The NBR announced the decision in a notice issued Monday.
According to the notice, an unusually high number of concurrent users accessed the eVAT system on November 15, 2026, causing server complications that prevented many taxpayers from submitting their returns within the stipulated deadline.
Considering the difficulties faced by taxpayers and in the public interest, the revenue authority extended the deadline by exercising its statutory authority.
The extension will give businesses and other VAT-registered taxpayers additional time to complete their online filing without facing interest or penalties.

item.title: BB: 15 banks account for 85% of Bangladesh’s default loans
item.description:
A total of 15 banks, including five merged Shariah-based banks, were behind more than 85% of the over Tk600,000 crore in non-performing loans (NPLs), said the Bangladesh Bank.
They also observed that asset-quality distress remains concentrated in a handful of lenders rather than being widespread across the banking sector.
The latest Bangladesh Bank Quarterly report for April-June 2026, published Monday, showed that total classified loans across the country’s 61 scheduled commercial banks rose in the fourth quarter of FY26 from more than Tk588,700 crore in the previous quarter.
This pushed the aggregate gross NPL ratio to 32.78% from 32.26% in the preceding quarter, driven by a moderate increase in the ratio among state-owned banks.
Not all commercial lenders contributed equally to the banking sector’s distress, the BB report found.
Excluding the five recently merged Shariah-based banks, 10 other banks held more than 57% of total classified loans.
This suggested that the distressed-asset problem is concentrated in a few banks rather than being pervasive across the sector, the central bank said.
The central bank said the banking sector continued to face structural challenges stemming from persistent weaknesses in asset quality, capital adequacy and profitability.
“Although excess liquidity provided some relief and signalled improved depositors’ confidence, the weakening performance indicators show that further action is needed to address vulnerabilities, improve risk management and strengthen sector resilience,” it added.
Apart from asset-quality pressures, capital adequacy in the banking sector deteriorated further in the fourth quarter of FY26, the BB said.
The Capital-to-Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR), which measures a bank’s available capital against its total risk-weighted assets, also weakened during the quarter.
The CRAR deficit widened to 3.80 percent at the end of the quarter from 3.17% in the previous quarter, taking the ratio further below the Basel III regulatory minimum requirement of 10%.
Across bank categories, the CRAR of state-owned banks fell to 0.82% at the end of the fourth quarter of FY26 from 1.08% in the previous quarter, remaining substantially below the regulatory requirement.
The capital adequacy ratio of private banks declined to 8.18% in April-June 2026 from 9.11% in the previous quarter.
The central bank said capital adequacy at Shariah-based banks also remained under significant pressure. Excluding the five merged Islamic banks, the CRAR of the remaining shariah-based banks fell to 7.30% from 7.75% in the preceding quarter.
Full-fledged Shariah-based banks collectively accounted for more than 47% of the banking industry’s total stock of defaulted loans in the fourth quarter of FY26, mainly because of high NPLs at the five merged Islamic institutions.
The BB’s initiatives to offer an exit facility to defaulting borrowers and recover defaulted loans under the proposed Distressed Asset Management Act 2026 and the proposed amendment to the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003, alongside other regulatory reforms, are expected to restore discipline in the sector in the near future.

item.title: ADB willing to support Bangladesh’s capital market
item.description:
The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has expressed keen interest in supporting the development of Bangladesh’s capital market, opening up prospects for greater institutional cooperation, private sector investment and expanded public-private partnerships (PPPs) to strengthen the country's investment ecosystem.
A high-level ADB delegation led by Takeo Koike, head of the ADB's Office of Markets Development and Public-Private Partnership (OMDP), conveyed the interest during a meeting with Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (BSEC) Chairman Masud Khan at the commission's office in the capital on Monday.
The discussions focused on the potential areas of cooperation between the securities regulator and the Manila-based multilateral development lender, particularly in strengthening the institutional capacity of the capital market, promoting private sector development and creating new avenues for investment, said a BSEC statement.
The ADB's interest comes at a time when Bangladesh needs a stronger and more diversified capital market to mobilize long-term financing for businesses, reduce excessive dependence on bank borrowing and support private sector-led economic growth.
During the meeting, the BSEC chief outlined various initiatives undertaken by the current commission to develop, expand and modernize the country's capital market, along with its future plans.
He also highlighted the importance of making the capital market more vibrant and effective in supporting private sector expansion and generating new investment opportunities.
The ADB delegation expressed its willingness to work with Bangladesh in advancing capital market development.
The potential areas of engagement included enhancing institutional capabilities, facilitating private sector growth and exploring opportunities to strengthen PPP initiatives.
The discussions also covered how the capital market could play a greater role in supporting investment and broadening financing opportunities for the country’s businesses.
The BSEC assured the ADB delegation of providing necessary cooperation in pursuing collaborative initiatives for the development of the country’s capital market.
Both sides held discussions on various aspects of market development and possible avenues for future cooperation.

item.title: UN: Drones behind nearly 75% of civilian deaths this year in Sudan war
item.description:
Drones caused nearly three quarters of all the verified civilian fatalities this year in the war in Sudan, the UN said Tuesday.
The war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) erupted in April 2023 and is estimated to have killed more than 200,000 people in total.
The conflict has forced more than 13 million to flee their homes, creating the world's largest hunger and displacement crisis, according to aid groups.
Out of 2,230 civilian deaths confirmed by the UN human rights office Ohchr to have occurred this year between January and end of October, more than 1,630 were a result of drone attacks, it said on Tuesday.
Drone attacks have "eclipsed the use of other tactics and weaponry," it said, adding that the full civilian casualty figures are likely to be higher.
Both warring parties have increasingly relied on drones capable of striking targets hundreds of kilometers away.
In a report on the human rights situation in Sudan, Ohchr said the first six months of the year were marked by an "unmistakable increase in drone strikes against civilians and civilian objects."
The use of drones has now become "one of the defining features of the conflict," it said.
With the war well into its fourth year, "a robust war economy and steady supply of weapons and other external support enabled the parties to sustain fighting as the conflict continued to spread and evolve," the report said.
The conflict is exacting an "unbearable toll" on civilians, while the prospects for a ceasefire and a peaceful resolution to the conflict remain elusive, it said.
From January 1 to June 30, Ohchr said it continued to document indiscriminate attacks, reprisals against civilians accused of collaborating with opposing forces, and the widespread use of sexual violence as a weapon of war.
Civilians in the Kordofan region accounted for more than two-thirds of documented casualties, followed by Darfur, where most of the remaining casualties occurred.
"The findings in our report provide more evidence, if any were needed, of the ceaselessly unbearable civilian suffering of the war in Sudan and the warring parties' continued and brazen disregard for the laws of war," UN rights chief Volker Turk said in a statement.
"Amid pervasive impunity, the report documents, once again, serious violations of international humanitarian law. Such violations may amount to war crimes."
The intensification of drone strikes targeting power stations and fuel supplies had become a "worrying trend," the report said.
Between October 20 and November 4, some 29 drone strikes, attributed to the RSF, hit electricity facilities and fuel stations, "triggering widespread power blackouts and further fuel shortages affecting millions far from the conflict frontlines," it said.
"These drone strikes had a devastating impact on civilians and essential services, " it said.
"The parties to the conflict must protect civilians and uphold their international law obligations -- the world is watching," Turk said.

item.title: Board chief: New garment wages to take effect from Dec 1, regardless of announcement date
item.description:
New wages for garment workers will take effect from December 1, regardless of when they are officially announced, Minimum Wage Board Chairman Syed Azad Subhani said on Tuesday.
He urged workers not to be misled by rumours, misinformation or fake notices regarding the wage announcement and called on them to avoid creating disorder.
He made the remarks at a briefing at the Minimum Wage Board office in Segunbagicha in the capital.
Subhani said the board's scheduled meeting on Monday was postponed after one of its representatives fell ill. The meeting will now be held on November 23.
Reiterating the implementation timeline, he said the new minimum wages would come into effect from December 1, irrespective of the announcement date.
The government formed a six-member Minimum Wage Board for garment workers on November 1. A tripartite emergency meeting involving representatives of workers, employers and the government was also held on the same day.
Despite these initiatives, workers' protests have continued in several areas. In response, the government has stepped up security in industrial zones, deploying police, Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) and Armed Police Battalion (APBn) personnel.

item.title: CPD proposes Tk 18,578–Tk 24,204 wage range for garment workers
item.description:
The non-government think-tank, Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), believes that wage negotiations for workers in the readymade garment (RMG) industry should be based on a range of Tk 18,000 to Tk 24,000.

Nazneen Ahmed, executive director of the CPD, presented the findings of a report at a media briefing titled ‘Fair Wages in the RMG Sector: Issues for Consideration’, organised by the organisation on Wednesday morning.

CPD Distinguished Fellows Debapriya Bhattacharya and Mustafizur Rahman, and Head of Research Towfiqul Islam, among others, were present at the briefing.

Nazneen Ahmed said, “Considering the poverty line, the wage required for a worker should be Tk 18,578. The living wage, meanwhile, stands at Tk 24,204. Our central point is that discussions on wages should take place within the range between these two figures.”

“We believe our goal over time should be to move towards ensuring a living wage for workers. In other words, we need to ensure a wage that enables workers to maintain adequate nutrition and lead a humane and dignified life. We believe this broader objective should also be taken into account when determining wages,” she further said.

The CPD executive director added, “We would rather not use the term ‘bargaining’. Instead, we are proposing that an acceptable wage be determined within the range of Tk 18,578 to Tk 24,204 through reviews and discussions between the two parties.”

The government formed a minimum wage board for garment workers on 1 November. Two meetings have already been held. 

At the second meeting, the workers’ representatives proposed a minimum monthly wage of Tk 32,000. At the third meeting, scheduled for last Monday, the employers’ side was expected to present its wage proposal, but the meeting was postponed. The next meeting is scheduled for 23 November.

Meanwhile, garment workers have been staging protests in different parts of the country for more than a month, demanding higher wages. The current minimum monthly wage for garment workers is Tk 12,500. The revised wage structure came into effect on 1 December 2023.

Govt working to cap migration cost for Malaysia at Tk 200,000: PM
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Wednesday said the government has restarted sending Bangladeshi workers to Malaysia and has largely managed to keep the total cost of going there within Tk 200,000 per worker.

“The government has, by and large, been able to keep the total migration cost for a worker going to Malaysia within Tk 200,000,” he told the Jatiya Sangsad (JS).

The premier made the remarks while responding to a starred supplementary question from Mymensingh-6 lawmaker Md Kamrul Hasan during the Prime Minister’s question-answer session.

He said the government is giving special priority to bringing down the overall migration cost, including travel expenses, for Bangladeshi workers seeking employment abroad.

Referring to talks with Malaysia on resuming the suspended recruitment, Tarique Rahman said, “By the grace of Allah, the government has been able to restart the process.”

He added that the government’s discussions and initiatives are continuing to keep migration costs at an affordable level for Bangladeshi workers in other Middle Eastern countries as well.

Efforts are also underway to keep the cost of going abroad within Tk 200,000, or at least at a bearable level, in those countries, said the prime minister.

Tarique Rahman said the syndicate problem and the defrauding of job seekers, raised by the lawmaker, had reached its worst under the fugitive autocrat’s regime.

“We saw how people linked to them swindled citizens with promises of jobs abroad and pocketed their money,” he said.

He said the syndicates built by that regime had also damaged Bangladesh’s standing abroad, and several countries had almost stopped recruiting Bangladeshi workers, suspending intake or slowing it down.

Deputy Speaker Kayser Kamal was in the chair as the sitting began at 4:15 pm. The first 30 minutes were allotted for the Prime Minister’s questions.

The fourth session of the JS began on 9 November. As per a decision of the Business Advisory Committee, the short session is scheduled to end today with the Prime Minister’s concluding speech.

item.title: Rooppur plant delivers 350MW to national grid in 8.5hrs
item.description:
The first unit of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant supplied 350 megawatts of electricity to the national grid during an eight-and-a-half-hour trial run on Tuesday, marking its first power injection into the grid.
The unit operated without any reported problems before being disconnected for further technical tests. It will be run again for several hours, although the date of the next trial has not yet been fixed.
Project Director Kabir Hossain told Dhaka Tribune that the plant had completed the initial run successfully. Power generation would be increased gradually, depending on the results of further tests.
The trial supply began at 3:16pm on Tuesday in the presence of Science and Technology Minister Faqir Mahbub Anam.
During the tests, engineers monitored the performance and stability of the turbine, generator and systems connecting the plant to the national grid.
Project officials said each stage would assess the plant’s systems, turbine and generator performance, and grid integration. If the results are satisfactory, the plant will require approval from the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) before the next phase of trial operations.
Under an agreement with the Russian contractor, the first unit is expected to undergo a 10-month trial operation before beginning commercial power supply at full capacity.
Following the trial period, the unit will be provisionally handed over by the Russian contractor to the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission. The Nuclear Power Plant Company Bangladesh Ltd (NPCBL) will subsequently begin operating the facility through a government gazette notification.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,329 as six die in 24 hours
item.description:
Six more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Wednesday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 1,329.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all six of the latest casualties as suspected.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,224, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 105, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
Among the six new suspected fatalities, the highest concentration was recorded in Dhaka, with three deaths reported in both the Dhaka division and Dhaka district.
A total of 1,376 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Wednesday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 252,173.
During the same period, 258 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 25,786.
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 225,339 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 216,389 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS.

item.title: RMG unrest escalates, 300 arrested as clashes spread
item.description:
Garment workers’ protests demanding a Tk30,000 minimum monthly wage intensified across Dhaka, Gazipur, Savar and Ashulia on Wednesday, triggering fresh clashes with police, highway blockades and factory closures, while nearly 300 people have been arrested in connection with the continuing unrest.
The escalating confrontation, now in its third week, has disrupted production across Bangladesh’s largest export industry, with workers accusing authorities of delaying wage negotiations and police stepping up operations to contain the violence.
In Gazipur, thousands of workers blocked the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway around 9am, bringing traffic to a standstill in Chhaydana, Hariken and surrounding industrial areas.
A vehicle belonging to Gazipur Metropolitan Police was set ablaze during clashes.
Police confirmed the arson, while law enforcement personnel worked to disperse protesters and restore traffic, which normalised after 2pm.
At least 20 factories in Savar and Ashulia remained closed amid the unrest, while several factories in Gazipur also suspended operations.
In Savar’s Ulail area, thousands of workers from Al-Muslim Group and nearby factories blocked the Dhaka-Aricha highway around 2:30pm.
Clashes erupted when police attempted to clear the road. Officers fired tear gas and rubber bullets after protesters allegedly threw bricks, forcing workers to retreat around 4pm.
Similar confrontations occurred in Ashulia’s Narsinghapur area, where police used tear gas to disperse workers attempting to block the Abdullahpur-Baipail road. Several people, including police personnel, were injured.
In the capital, garment workers clashed with police in Pallabi and became involved in confrontations with local BNP activists in Kafrul following allegations that female workers had been harassed.
Police used sound grenades to restore order.
Police said nearly 300 people had been arrested in 24 cases filed with Savar and Ashulia police stations over alleged sabotage during the continuing protests.
Two leaders of the Green Bangla Garments Workers Federation were also arrested in Dhaka on Tuesday night on allegations of inciting unrest.
The unrest intensified after the minimum wage board postponed its third meeting, scheduled for November 16. The meeting has now been rescheduled for November 23.
Workers are demanding an increase in the minimum wage from Tk12,500 to Tk30,000, arguing that rising living costs have eroded their purchasing power.
Labour leaders say uncertainty over the wage board’s proceedings has fuelled mistrust among workers, who want the new wage structure announced before December and implemented from December 1.
Meanwhile, lawmakers from both treasury and opposition benches have expressed support for a reasonable wage increase while alleging that vested interests, including elements linked to the ousted Awami League, are attempting to exploit the unrest.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed told the National Parliament that some groups were deliberately prolonging the protests despite ongoing negotiations between workers and factory owners.

item.title: US, China can help end Ukraine war, Trump tells Xi before trilateral with Putin
item.description:
TOPSHOT-CHINA-APEC-SUMMIT-DIPLOMACY

  • Trump says US, China can help end war in Ukraine

  • Trump calls Putin a “friend”

  • Trump meets Xi, Putin separately before unprecedented trilateral

  • Analysts say gathering is unlikely to produce major agreements

US President Donald Trump told his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping on Thursday that they should both help end the war in Ukraine ahead of their unprecedented three-way meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The diplomatic gathering of the leaders of the world’s largest nuclear powers is unlikely to produce major agreements, analysts say, given deep differences over Ukraine, Iran, nuclear weapons and trade. But it has unnerved smaller countries that fear their interests might be disregarded.

Trump met Putin and Xi separately ahead of the trilateral talks, calling the Russian leader a “friend”. The Kremlin said they discussed Ukraine and that Putin left the meeting in an “excellent” mood.

When meeting Xi right after, Trump thanked him for a lavish welcome and expressed hope that their trilateral with Putin would be successful.

“We’re looking to both help with respect to the war with Russia and Ukraine,” Trump said. “I’d like to see it ended.”

Trump said both presidents felt strongly about oil having to flow through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been disrupted by the Iran war. Xi did not mention Ukraine or Iran in his remarks.

Patricia Kim, foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution, said China would not want to be seen as brokering a deal over Ukraine, given the “problematic optics” of Kyiv and European leaders not taking part.

“Xi has characterized the Russia-Ukraine war as fundamentally a European problem, making Beijing even less inclined to assume responsibility for resolving it,” Kim said.

Fanfare and pageantry

Speaking to Fox News earlier on Thursday, Trump highlighted the pomp surrounding his arrival for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, which contrasted with the more muted greeting of other leaders, including Putin. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi landed without any welcoming ceremony.

Japan’s relations with China have soured since Takaichi’s remarks in 2025, when she said Japan could deploy its military if a Chinese move on Taiwan also threatened its territory.

On Thursday, she said Tokyo’s position on Taiwan had not changed.

Taiwan’s defence ministry said two Russian military aircraft flew to the island’s east on Thursday.

Xi greeted Trump at the airport, the first time he has done so with any visiting leader since ‌becoming president, reciprocating his counterpart’s gesture at Joint Base Andrews in September when they last met. The leaders also briefly hugged.

“This is a great president, one of the great presidents of China, and he’s never gone to the airport to meet somebody,” Trump said, when asked what he wanted to get out of the trilateral.

“And not only that, the fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people, the young children, the soldiers, the whole thing. It was great respect, and I appreciate that. That’s a big win for us. It’s a big win for China too.”

Trump arrived after Xi and Putin delivered pointed speeches denouncing Western trade “protectionism” and sanctions.

During Thursday’s APEC proceedings, Xi called for “free and open” trade. Western leaders say China’s growth model favouring industrial strength over consumers is unfair and creates destabilising global trade imbalances.

Putin, fresh from a setback in his war against Ukraine after the crippling of a key bridge linking Crimea to Russia, said Russia was key for food and energy security in the Asia-Pacific.

Trump told the audience the US has been a Pacific power for hundreds of years and touted the strength of its economy.

Tough nuclear arms discussion

Trump has insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit, despite China’s repeated objections to joining talks with Washington and Moscow, which have far larger nuclear arsenals.

The president has also expressed interest in meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, but there was no confirmation of an imminent encounter.

Trump’s Asia trip has offered a chance to showcase US influence, strengthen ties with regional allies and pursue a high-profile diplomatic opening with Xi and Putin.

But the US president will return home facing political challenges, including the fallout from bruising midterm elections, the Nvidia spy scandal and a spate of tech and air travel outages that have rattled Americans.

The leaders have plenty of reasons to appear together but far fewer to agree on substance, given differences over Ukraine, Iran, nuclear weapons, trade and China’s military buildup, said Craig Singleton of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.

“A photograph could serve all three men well,” Singleton said, adding that he thought the “agenda is much harder to agree on.”

Trump’s talks with Xi come after an extension of their trade truce this month, but also amid growing tension over reports of Nvidia chips being diverted to China through Southeast Asia, raising questions about the effectiveness of US export curbs and the future of Chinese access to advanced technology.

“This is Beijing’s worst nightmare. China wants chip access that it can negotiate with the president. It may get chip restrictions written into law by both parties,” Singleton said.

item.title: Mideast crisis ‘largest threat’ to energy security ever: IEA
item.description:
IRAN-CRISIS/INSURANCE-SHIPPING

The crisis in the Middle East sparked in February by the US and Israeli bombing of Iran has created the “largest threat” to energy security in history, the International Energy Agency (IEA) warned Thursday.

The agency said in its flagship annual World Energy Outlook that consumers were increasingly footing the bill as the world runs out of ways to absorb the impact of the conflict on energy supplies.

The crisis, just like previous energy shocks, would certainly leave “lasting marks”, the agency warned.

Gulf countries have been struggling to export oil since Iran began blockading the Strait of Hormuz and targeting tankers in the area, following US and Israeli strikes that sparked the crisis in February.

Despite attempts by the United States to escort vessels through the channel -- which pre-crisis carried about one-fifth of global oil shipments -- supply lines remain severely disrupted.

“The Strait of Hormuz crisis has created the largest threat to energy security in history, one that dwarfs the scale of the oil shocks of the 1970s,” IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol wrote in his foreword to the report.

He highlighted the efforts countries had taken to protect households, with producing nations bringing more supplies into the market and using alternative routes, and China buying less from international markets.

“Governments have intervened to try and provide some shelter for consumers, but they have nonetheless faced higher prices and, in some cases, shortfalls of supply,” Birol wrote.

The report said elsewhere that “increasingly it is falling to consumers -- and high prices -- to absorb the impact as other buffers are run down”.

Birol had struck a more hopeful tone in July when he wrote that the oil market was still benefiting from “several cushioning factors”.

‘No pathway’ back

 The IEA’s report comes as nations meet for the COP31 climate talks in Turkey, with governments under pressure to tackle climate change after a year of searing heatwaves and wildfires in Europe, and deadly floods in Nepal.

The agency uses three scenarios for its energy outlook: a cautious one takes into account policies that are currently in place, a middle scenario looks at “stated” government policies including measures that have yet to be adopted, and a third considers a world that reaches net zero emissions by 2050.

In its middle scenario, the IEA forecasts that global oil demand will reach a peak around 2030 before a slow decline, while gas demand would increase until around 2035.

For this report, it also adds two other scenarios based on what might happen if the Middle East crisis persists.

“While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be,” Birol said in a press release.

“And I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before.”

item.title: An agreement needed before the Ganges Water Treaty expires
item.description:
The Ganges treaty between Bangladesh and India is set to expire in a few days on 12 December. There has been no news of a new agreement or the renewal of the existing one. It is also unclear whether the two countries are willing to agree on an interim arrangement. The situation is concerning, but people downstream still hold hope.

The first Ganges treaty was signed in 1977. Those who are older might remember the intense political situation in the years leading up to it, particularly surrounding the "Farakka" issue. A few years went by without an agreement even at the end of the last century. During that time, water politics were intense, but the branches of the Ganges in Bangladesh started drying up. The potential lack of an agreement this time could be the final nail in the coffin for these narrow rivers.

As I write this, there is not enough time left for a new agreement. The alternatives are to either have a temporary memorandum of understanding based on the main conditions of the old agreement or renew the agreement for two to three years, as permitted by Article 12. Are the two governments in discussions about such an option? Will they take such a step?

If the potential for such an emergency memorandum slips away due to the uncertainty surrounding Bangladesh's Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's visit to India, it would be disastrous for the region's ecology. Any poor agreement would be preferable to having no agreement at all, especially for those downstream.

The Bangladesh government says they want a new agreement. It should certainly include additional elements compared to the 1996 treaty. At the same time, it should also include more than the 1977 agreement. In that case, a comparative discussion of both agreements is needed. The first treaty was for five years. The second was for 30 years, which was an advancement, but a permanent agreement would be better in the future, with opportunities for review from time to time. Both previous agreements aimed to address the five months of the dry season (January-May). A future agreement should cover the entire year, including flood management strategies, which is also crucial for those downstream.

In 1977, there was an "Agreement" on the Ganges, and the subsequent one was a "Treaty". The first one was signed by ministers, and the second by prime ministers. It is evident that as time has passed, the commitment on water issues between the two countries has deepened. However, there was no provision for an "arbitrator" in either agreement. Including such a provision in the future would be beneficial.

Relations with neighbors can rise and fall, but people in the basin cannot be put at risk in critical matters like water. Therefore, if there is a dispute over water rights, there should be an option to call a third party as an arbitrator. It would also be beneficial to include Nepal in any potential agreement, as they are a strong partner in the flow of the Ganges. If an agreement could be reached among the three countries, the sense of trust among people downstream would increase. Both the 1977 and 1996 agreements considered water availability at the "Farakka Point, " which is harmful to Bangladesh.

In the future, the priority should be to keep the entire flow of the Ganges normal and ensure a fair share for Bangladesh based on that flow. If Bangladesh raises such a demand, India might be unhappy because they have built many infrastructures upstream over the past 40 years that are reducing the river's flow. In such a situation, an alternative for Bangladesh could be to approach the United Nations. Before doing so, it is also necessary to sign the UN's 1997 Watercourses Convention. Because Bangladesh has not signed it, India cannot be pressured to sign it either. It is a significant puzzle why Bangladesh has not yet signed a convention that could be in its national interest.

Dhaka desires a "guarantee clause" as an assurance of minimum water availability in any new agreement. It was present in Article 2 of the 1977 agreement and also differently in Articles 10 and 11 of the 1996 agreement. Therefore, there is no issue including it in the future, and it is crucial for downstream interests. However, over the past 30 to 40 years, the flow of water reaching Farakka has significantly decreased. While the concept of a guarantee clause exists in the agreement documents, only "apolitical" experts could propose how to implement it practically in the riverbed. Indian experts, in particular, suggest they need an additional 5,000 cusecs beyond the previous agreement's allocation.

Currently, there is much speculation in Bangladesh about the future of water distribution. The most pessimistic prediction is that there will be little response from India for a new agreement with more favorable terms for those downstream. The somewhat optimistic reverse prediction is that if this December ends without even a memorandum of understanding, it will be harmful to India as well. It is expected that anti-India sentiment will resurface in Bangladesh, which many in New Delhi likely do not want.

Secondly, Farakka has already caused significant and irreparable harm to the neighboring states of Bihar and West Bengal. Continuing to stop water in the future would bring additional damage to these two states.
Yet, the objections rising in Bihar and West Bengal over a new treaty and the renewal of the old one is itself a puzzle. Perhaps BJP's "political calculations" are at play, which Bangladesh should smartly consider. Perhaps these "movements" are part of negotiations with Dhaka.

For the first time in history, the BJP rules simultaneously in Kolkata, Patna, and New Delhi. This is a good time for any new water agreement because a Delhi-Dhaka understanding is now sufficient. However, at the same time, Bangladesh-India relations are at a historical low, which is a bad time for any new treaty. In this contradictory situation, it is also true that New Delhi's Bangladesh-oriented diplomacy over the past one and a half decades is facing a comprehensive reassessment as we approach 2024.

They clearly indicate a desire to rebuild this relationship. They might also consider the Ganges treaty as part of new "understandings and arrangements" under these new circumstances. Therefore, this moment could be turned into an opportunity for Bangladesh. The agreements of 1977 and 1996 were made in November-December, and moving toward potential prospects in the same season in 2026 might be possible.

Although determining water and water rights is entirely a technical matter, any water agreement comes to fruition only with the conscious touch of politicians. If the BJP government wants to view any potential new treaty as part of a larger political package, it could be uncomfortable for Bangladesh. However, what other choice is there but to face that reality?

The only feasible priority for popular politicians could be to blindly prioritize the protection of ecological interests. Although the opposition parties in Bangladesh are currently silent, they will begin to blame the government for failure as soon as the current treaty expires without any alternative agreement. Therefore, an interim arrangement could only be protective for both Dhaka and Delhi.

Bangladesh could achieve 5.7pc annual growth through fiscal reforms: WB
item.description:
Bangladesh could raise its annual economic growth to 5.7 per cent by boosting domestic revenue, rationalising subsidies, making public spending more efficient and reforming energy pricing, according to a latest World Bank report.

The report titled 'Bangladesh Public Finance Review, 2026' also said if fully implemented, reforms could raise revenue from 8 percent of GDP in FY2025 to 14.4 per cent by FY2035, compared with 10 per cent under limited reforms scenario.

Public spending could rise to 18 per cent of GDP, and the fiscal deficit would stay below 5 per cent throughout and fall to 3.6 per cent by FY2035, it added.

The report mentioned these reforms would build foundations for Bangladesh remain on inclusive growth path and create more and better jobs.

The World Bank’s report finds that low revenues, rising recurrent spending, and growing energy sector fiscal pressures are limiting development spending, particularly investments in human development and infrastructure.

The report also recommends more targeted subsidies, which will protect poor and vulnerable households.

Immediate and sequenced reforms to strengthen revenue mobilisation, improve the efficiency and allocation of public spending, address energy sector fiscal risks will create greater fiscal space for investment in infrastructure and human capital and help Bangladesh return to an inclusive growth path.

Fiscal reform must become a central pillar of the country's growth and jobs strategy, and it is essential to the government's goal of a trillion-dollar economy by 2034.

Key findings:

The economy is not generating enough jobs for its young and growing labour force.

Three in five working-age women are outside the labour force, and 84 per cent of workers are in informal jobs.

Slowing job creation reflects chronic government underinvestment in skills, infrastructure, and reliable energy, which have undermined private sector development

Revenue is very low. Taxes were 6.8 per cent of GDP in FY2025. Total revenue was 8 per cent, less than half the level of peer countries.

Public investment has been squeezed. Capital spending fell from 4.9 per cent of GDP in FY2022 to 2.8 per cent in FY2025. Education spending (1.5 per cent of GDP in FY2025) is well below that of peers.

Debt costs are rising. Interest payments rose from 1.5 per cent of GDP in FY2017 to an estimated 2.6 per cent in FY2026. Heavy borrowing from domestic banks is crowding out private credit.

Energy subsidies are a growing fiscal drain. Power and gas subsidies rose from 0.3 per cent of GDP in FY2018 to 1.5 per cent in FY2025. Recent global energy price spikes are expected to push them higher.

Reforms Needed for Enhancing Fiscal Space

Strengthen revenue governance and modernise tax administration. This means separating tax policy from tax administration, integrating digital systems and moving to a single taxpayer ID.

Streamline tax exemptions and reform VAT and trade taxes. Tax expenditures reached 6.9 per cent of GDP in FY2022, almost as much as total tax revenue.

Move to cost-reflective, rules-based energy pricing. Pair pricing reform with a stronger and more independent energy regulator.

Protect poor households while reforming energy pricing.

Targeted transfers, a stronger social registry and the Family Card platform would replace broad subsidies. Poverty headcount is estimated to have risen from 18.7 per cent in 2022 to 22.5 per cent in 2026. The report is clear that reform needs to improve the effectiveness of support, not reduce protection for vulnerable groups.

Invest more and spend better. Fiscal space created by reform could go to health, education, social protection and infrastructure, supported by better planning and budgeting.

item.title: 10,000 constable, 4,000 SI posts approved: How will the recruitment process work?
item.description:
All administrative hurdles to large-scale recruitment in the Bangladesh Police have been cleared as the government has finalised the approval to recruit 10,000 constables and 4,000 sub-inspectors (SIs) directly.

There are now no remaining obstacles to recruiting a total of 14,000 personnel.

All official procedures, including approval from the Ministry of Public Administration, the Ministry of Finance and the Secretaries Committee, have already been completed.

As a result, the Bangladesh Police can formally begin the recruitment process at any time.

The final approval has created a major opportunity for those who have been preparing to join the police force for a long time. Notably, this is the first time all 4,000 SI posts are being filled through direct recruitment.

The Police Regulations of Bengal (PRB) have been amended for this purpose. Previously, 50 per cent of SI posts were filled through departmental promotions and the remaining 50 per cent through direct recruitment.

Besides, the government is also considering holding a special Bangladesh Civil Service (BCS) examination to recruit 400 to 500 officers to the post of assistant superintendent of police (ASP)

Current status of the recruitment process

Asked about the latest developments and administrative preparations for the large-scale police recruitment, Tanvir-Al-Nasif, deputy secretary at the Ministry of Home Affairs, told Prothom Alo on Thursday that there were no longer any obstacles to starting the recruitment process.

He said all administrative procedures for recruiting 10,000 constables and 4,000 SIs had been completed, including approval from the Ministry of Public Administration, the Ministry of Finance and the Secretaries Committee. The Bangladesh Police can now begin the recruitment process at any time.

Meanwhile, Kamarum Munira, assistant inspector general (Media and Public Relations) at Police Headquarters, provided details about the ongoing constable recruitment circular. She told Prothom Alo that a total of 102,694 jobseekers from across the country had applied online under the ongoing circular.

Explaining the recruitment plan, Kamarum Munira further said there were currently 2,000 vacant constable posts in the police force. In addition, approval had been granted to recruit 10,000 new constables.

Considering the recruitment process, the plan is to fill the existing 2,000 vacancies along with another 4,000 posts from the newly approved 10,000 through the ongoing recruitment circular. This means a total of 6,000 constables are likely to be recruited through the current process. The remaining 6,000 newly approved constable posts will be filled gradually through subsequent recruitment circulars.

Earlier, a recruitment circular for constables across the country was published on 9 October. Although applications closed on 30 October, the circular did not specify the number of posts. However, if the number of posts increases to 6,000, competition among candidates will be considerably lower than in the previous recruitment drive.

In the recruitment circular issued in April, 126,000 applications were submitted against 2,703 posts. At the time, 47 candidates were supposed to compete for each post. With the increase in the number of posts this time, an average of only 17 candidates will compete for each position.

How the recruitment selection process works

Candidates for constable and SI posts in the police force are selected through a rigorous screening process. For constable posts, candidates must pass preliminary screening, physical measurement, physical endurance tests, a written examination and a psychological test.

Recruitment for SI posts, on the other hand, is completed in several stages. Initially, applicants undergo physical measurement and document verification. They must then pass running and physical fitness tests. In the next stage, candidates sit for a written examination and a computer proficiency test. Finally, the Police Headquarters selects candidates through intelligence and viva voce tests.

For both positions, candidates will be screened based on merit and qualifications as well as intelligence reports. If an applicant provides false information in the application or at any stage of the selection process, their candidature will be cancelled immediately.

An SI serves as a highly important field-level officer in the police administration. Maintaining general diaries (GDs) at police stations and investigating criminal cases are among their primary responsibilities. They also work directly in the field to prevent crime, collect intelligence, arrest suspects and maintain overall law and order in their respective areas.

Grades and benefits of SI and constable posts

Sub-inspectors (SIs) and constables are two important positions in maintaining law and order at the field level in the country.

According to the national pay scale, an SI is a Grade 10 government employee. The starting basic salary for the position is Tk 32,000, rising to a maximum of Tk 77,300.

On the other hand, a trainee recruit constable (TRC) falls under Grade 17. After completing training and receiving permanent appointment, a constable receives a starting basic salary of Tk 9,000, rising to a maximum of Tk 21,800.

In addition to their basic salaries, both SIs and constables receive several allowances and benefits under government regulations. These include house rent allowance depending on the area of posting, medical allowance, risk allowance, festival allowance, and tiffin and travel allowances.

They are also provided with uniforms free of cost at government expense, subsidised ration facilities for themselves and their families, and advanced medical services. During training, they also receive prescribed allowances and accommodation facilities.

Based on merit and qualifications, employees in both positions have opportunities for promotion to higher ranks in the future.

item.title: Tulip Siddiq plans to sue former interim govt chief Yunus
item.description:
Former British minister Tulip Siddiq has said she plans to take legal action against former Bangladesh interim government chief Professor Muhammad Yunus, accusing his administration of malicious prosecution over corruption allegations.

“I had been the victim of a malicious prosecution,” the Guardian quoted her as telling Politics Unleashed.

Siddiq resigned from the UK government amid allegations that she had benefited from her aunt Sheikh Hasina’s regime in Bangladesh.

In December 2025, a Bangladeshi court sentenced her to two years in prison after trying her in absentia in a corruption case.

She was found guilty of influencing Hasina to secure a plot of land for her family on the outskirts of Dhaka.

Siddiq has strongly denied the allegations and is unlikely to serve the sentence as she is based in London.

Denmark ratifies security deal with US and Greenland
item.description:
Denmark’s parliament on Thursday ratified a security agreement with the US over Greenland, hoping to end tensions after US President Donald Trump had repeatedly demanded control over the autonomous Danish territory.
In the Danish 179-seat parliament, all 109 members present voted in favor of the text. Greenland’s parliament already ratified the deal in early November.
US ambassador to Denmark, Kenneth Howery, welcomed the ratification, saying in a post on X: “The agreement is a tremendous accomplishment, one that modernizes our partnership for the security challenges of the future and bolsters the security of the United States, the Kingdom of Denmark, including Greenland, and all of Nato.”
The trilateral security and military access agreement between Washington, Nuuk and Copenhagen allows for expanded US military presence on the mineral-rich and strategically located island in the northern Atlantic.
It also includes permission to establish a “Golden ‌Dome” ​missile defense system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
The island is home to some 57,000 people and is strategically located along the shortest route from Europe to North America. It already is home to the northernmost US military base.
The deal was signed in September by Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen but still needed ratification from lawmakers in Greenland and Denmark.
In January 2026, Trump renewed calls for Greenland to become part of the US, threatening military action and tariffs against European allies if they opposed him.
He argued that Denmark was not able to protect the autonomous Arctic territory from threats by China and Russia. His demands strained US relations with Denmark and alarmed European Nato allies.
Tensions somewhat eased in late January when Trump and Nato Secretary-General Mark Rutte announced a “concept of a deal” that would expand US military access to Greenland. This then led to the agreement being signed in September.
Under a 1951 agreement, the US already has broad military access to Greenland. Denmark had repeatedly said it was open to expanding the US military presence on the island but rejected Trump’s demand for full US control.

item.title: Riyadh skyscraper damaged as Saudi reports new Houthi attacks
item.description:
A skyscraper in Riyadh housing the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund was damaged on Thursday, witnesses told AFP, as the kingdom reported new attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.
Saudi Arabia has been battling a surge in attacks since fighting reignited over the summer in neighboring Yemen’s civil war, where Riyadh backs the internationally recognized government against the Houthis.
In the early hours of Thursday, AFP journalists in the Saudi capital reported a powerful blast had been heard.
Around the same time, civil defense authorities issued a warning for “potential danger” but said minutes later that the danger had passed.
The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said it had “addressed a missile threat launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh”.
“Initial assessment indicates the impact of debris, with material damage currently being surveyed,” said coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki.
Witnesses later told AFP that Riyadh’s Public Investment Fund Tower, which at 80 stories is the tallest in the city’s financial district, had been damaged.
“The facade is damaged across several floors, with windows blown out,” said one source who requested anonymity. Two other sources confirmed the damage.
Standing 385 meters high, the tower dominates King Abdullah Financial District, which acts as a showcase for Saudi Arabia’s economic ambitions.
With imposing skyscrapers, luxury shops and green spaces, the district also hosts the headquarters of the Saudi stock exchange along with multinationals such as Goldman Sachs.
Chaired by Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the sovereign wealth fund is one of the largest in the world with more than $900 billion in assets under management.
It is also one of the main instruments for diversifying the kingdom’s economy away from oil, plans which have been threatened by the latest fighting.
Malki also said Thursday that the coalition had intercepted five ballistic missiles launched towards Saudi Arabia’s southern region, which borders Yemen.
The Iran-backed Houthis have stepped up their attacks against Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, striking targets including airports, energy infrastructure, military sites and Riyadh’s financial district.
In October, a deadly attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed 14 people and injured hundreds, forcing the suspension of flights for two weeks.
In response, the Saudi coalition has been striking Houthi targets in areas of Yemen held by the group.
On Thursday, Houthi media outlets reported that Saudi Arabia had launched another attack on Yemen’s capital Sanaa.
The Almasirah television channel said Saudi forces have “once again targeted the shoe and textile factory of the Alyateem Development Foundation,” citing its correspondent in Sanaa.
The Saudi coalition said it had “destroyed a ballistic missile launch platform in Dhamar,” a city about 100 kilometers (60 miles) south of Sanaa that was used by the Houthis to strike Riyadh.
The long-running civil war in Yemen, one of the world’s poorest countries, fell dormant in 2022 after a ceasefire was implemented, but sprang back to life this summer.
The Houthis are now nearing Aden, the internationally recognized government’s interim capital, having made sweeping territorial gains since the war resumed.
More than 1,600 people have been killed in the latest round of fighting and more than 300,000 displaced, according to the United Nations.
On Thursday, the Saudi crown prince met with US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper in Riyadh, according to state news agency SPA.
The two sides “reviewed bilateral relations, particularly in the military fields, and discussed regional developments”, the media outlet said.
On Wednesday, another powerful explosion rattled homes in Riyadh, with residents saying no mobile phone alerts were issued beforehand, as is usually the case.
“The explosion was extremely loud,” said one resident in the north of the city. “Hearing a blast without receiving a warning is very frightening.”
The coalition said it had intercepted two drones launched by the Houthis in the Riyadh and southern regions.
The military spokesman for the Houthis, Yahya Saree, said in a post on X that the group had targeted Riyadh’s international airport and the capital’s financial district with cruise missiles.
